diagnostic_evidence.quote: However, the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse is unique, so $\matR_{\va^\winv}= \matR_\vy$. Via the definitions of $\matR_\vy$ and $\matR_{\va^\winv}$, it is immediate that this implies that $\va^\winv=\vy$. Since $\vy$ is real, so is $\va^\winv$.

issues.failure_explanation: The proof claims that $\matR_\vy$ is the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of $\matR_\va$ and applies uniqueness of the pseudoinverse to conclude $\matR_{\va^\winv} = \matR_\vy$. The Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse conditions require the products to be Hermitian, i.e., $(\matR_\va \matX)^\ha = \matR_\va \matX$ and $(\matX \matR_\va)^\ha = \matX \matR_\va$. For a general invertible matrix $\matM$, $\matR_{\va \Mprod \vy} = \matM^{-1} \diag(\matM(\va \Mprod \vy)) \matM$ is not Hermitian or symmetric. Therefore, $\matR_\vy$ is not the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of $\matR_\va$, and uniqueness cannot be used to deduce $\matR_{\va^\winv} = \matR_\vy$.

failure_location.quote: The same four equation hold if we replace $\va$ with $\matR_\va$, $\vy$ with $\matR_\vy$ and $\Mprod$ with matrix product. Thus, $\matR_\vy$ is the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of $\matR_\va$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the pseudoinverse uniqueness argument by observing directly that since row pairs of $\matM$ are either real or conjugate pairs, $(\matM\va)^\pinv$ inherits the same conjugate-symmetry structure as $\matM\va$, which implies by Lemma 23 (lem:struct-Minv) that $\va^\winv = \matM^{-1}(\matM\va)^\pinv$ is real.
issues.overall_effect: The proof of Lemma 12 fails as written, leaving the premise that $\va^\winv \in \KM$ in Lemma 13 temporarily unestablished.
issues.title: Invalid proof of realness of weak inverse via Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse
issues.why_classification: The claim of Lemma 12 is true and follows by an immediate two-line consequence of Lemma 23 without needing any new proof machinery or weakening of results.

issues.failure_explanation: For any real tensor $\tenA \in \KM^{m\times p} \cong \R^{m\times p\times n}$, transformed frontal slices corresponding to complex conjugate rows $(j, l)$ of $\matM$ satisfy $\hat{\matA}_l = \overline{\hat{\matA}_j}$. When $r_j \neq r_l$, the independently truncated SVD slices have different ranks and cannot be complex conjugates, meaning that the reconstructed tensor $\lrapprox{\tenA}{\vr}$ is not real and does not belong to $\KM^{m\times p}$. Thus $\vr$ must satisfy $r_j = r_l$ for all conjugate pairs of rows in $\matM$. Additionally, because $\FnormS{\tenD} = |c|^{-2} \FnormS{\hat{\tenD}}$ by Lemma 21 (lem:added-4), the Frobenius squared error has scalar factor $|c|^{-2}$, not $|c|^{-1}$.

failure_location.quote: For any $n$-size tuple of non-negative integers $\vr$ such that $\vr \leq \Mmultirank(\tenA)$, we define the tensor $\lrapprox{\tenA}{\vr}$ as the tensor in which the frontal domain $j$ in the transformed space is the $r_j$ truncated SVD of the $j$th frontal face of the transformed $	enA$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the condition that $r_j = r_l$ whenever row $j$ and row $l$ of $\matM$ are complex conjugate pairs, and change the factor $|c|^{-1}$ to $|c|^{-2}$ in the squared error formula.
issues.overall_effect: Theorem 20 fails for arbitrary multirank tuples $\vr$ whenever $\matM$ has complex rows because the truncated tensor is non-real, and the stated approximation error formula has an incorrect power of $|c|$.
issues.title: Multirank Eckart-Young theorem omits conjugate symmetry and misstates error scaling
issues.why_classification: Adding the standard conjugate-symmetry condition on $\vr$ and correcting the exponent of $|c|$ fully restores the optimality guarantee and preserves the theorem's intended scope.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: The use of complex numbers is unavoidable. It can be shown that no such real $\matM$ exists.

issues.failure_explanation: The output contract of Algorithm 1 states that the returned matrix $\matM$ is in $\R^{n \times n}$. However, as Example 10 demonstrates and Theorem 14 formalizes, for any tubal ring whose realness is less than $n$ (such as rings containing complex subfields), no real matrix $\matM$ exists. For such rings, the eigendecomposition in line 7 yields complex eigenvectors and eigenvalues, producing a complex matrix $\matM \in \C^{n\times n}$ that violates the algorithm's contract.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Update the `Ensure` specification and the initialization in line 9 from $\matM \in \R^{n\times n}$ to $\matM \in \C^{n\times n}$.
issues.overall_effect: Algorithm 1 violates its output guarantee whenever applied to tubal rings that require complex $\matM$.
issues.title: Algorithm 1 output contract guarantees real matrix for complex tubal rings
issues.why_classification: The construction in Algorithm 1 correctly finds $\matM$; correcting the output field annotation from real to complex matrices resolves the defect without any algorithmic changes.
